paper_context.research_question: Can a fully non-monotonic transition system based on the non-projective Covington parser, trained with an approximate dynamic oracle using efficiently-computable loss bounds, improve parsing accuracy (and be practical to train) compared to monotonic and static oracles?
main_claims: A fully non-monotonic variant of the non-projective Covington transition system can be defined by allowing arc-creating transitions to overwrite previous heads and to break cycles via deterministic arc removal, enabling full repair of past attachments.

Exact loss computation for a non-monotonic non-projective parser is intractable/practically infeasible, but tight lower and upper bounds on loss can be computed efficiently and used to build an approximate dynamic oracle.

The proposed approximate non-monotonic dynamic oracle (with several loss-bound variants) yields tighter reachable-arc sets than the monotonic oracle and empirically produces better parsing accuracy on a majority of CoNLL-X / CoNLL-XI datasets.

Using the lower-bound loss makes training faster (oracle cheaper) and still competitive, while the upper-bound variant that counts cycles gives the best average accuracy despite being a cruder approximation in some respects.

This is the first implementation of full non-monotonicity for a non-projective parsing algorithm and the first practical approximate dynamic oracle based on close, efficiently-computable loss approximations.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Parsing accuracy (UAS and LAS) compared across static, monotonic-dynamic, and non-monotonic-dynamic oracles over multiple languages/datasets
Tightness of loss bounds: relative error of lower/upper bounds vs. exact loss (measured via exhaustive search on sampled transitions)
Practicality / runtime tradeoffs: oracle computation cost (lower-bound fast, cycle-counting upper-bound slower) and overall training time
Statistical significance of accuracy differences across seeds and datasets
Robustness across languages (variation and failure cases, e.g., observed Basque drop)
Theoretical/algorithmic soundness: correctness of transition definitions (single-head and acyclicity enforcement by arc removal) and consistency with non-projective parsing constraints

extracted_claims.claim_text: A fully non-monotonic variant of the non-projective Covington transition system can be defined by allowing Left-Arc and Right-Arc transitions to always create arcs (overwriting previous heads when present) and by enforcing acyclicity deterministically by removing a specific interfering arc when a newly-created arc would form a cycle.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Exact computation of the configuration loss for the fully non-monotonic non-projective Covington parser is intractable/practically infeasible, but tight lower and upper bounds on the loss can be computed efficiently and used instead.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 4 (Non-Monotonic Approximate Dynamic Oracle) and Section 5 (Evaluation of the loss bounds)

extracted_claims.claim_text: A non-monotonic approximate dynamic oracle built using the proposed loss bounds yields higher parsing accuracy than the monotonic dynamic oracle on a majority of CoNLL-X / CoNLL-XI datasets.
evidence: Section 6 and Table 3: non-monotonic oracle (with upper variant |U|+nc) improves over monotonic on 14 out of 19 languages and average UAS difference reported (0.32 UAS average vs monotonic).

Conclusion: "On average, our non-monotonic algorithm obtains better performance than the monotonic version, regardless of the loss calculation used."

extracted_claims.claim_label: lower bound fastest, upper bound best accuracy
extracted_claims.claim_text: Using the lower-bound loss makes training faster because the oracle is cheaper (no cycle computation), while the upper-bound variant that counts cycles (|U|+nc) gives the best average accuracy despite sometimes being a cruder approximation.

extracted_claims.claim_label: first full non-monotonic non-projective parser and oracle
extracted_claims.claim_text: This work presents the first implementation of full non-monotonicity for a non-projective parsing algorithm and the first practical approximate dynamic oracle based on tight, efficiently-computable loss approximations.
evidence: Introduction: "To our knowledge, the presented system is the first nonmonotonic parser that can produce non-projective dependency analyses."

Conclusion: "To our knowledge, this is the first implementation of non-monotonicity for a nonprojective parsing algorithm, and the first approximate dynamic oracle that uses close, efficiently-computable approximations of the loss."

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Removing the unique existing head z→x when a new arc x→y would create a cycle always enforces acyclicity while preserving the ability to later build any reachable gold arcs that are considered reachable under non-monotonicity.
supporting_evidence: Section 3: "if the creation of a new arc x→ y generates a cycle in A, we immediately remove the arc of the form z → x from A (which trivially exists, and is unique due to the single-head constraint)."
Figure 2 transitions showing set subtraction of previous head arcs.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If removing z→x breaks gold-foreseen paths or prevents reconstruction of certain gold arcs later (i.e., the deterministic removal interferes with optimal repair sequences), the computed reachable-arc sets and thus loss bounds would be incorrect, potentially biasing the oracle and harming training.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The three proposed loss expressions (lower bound |U|, upper bound |U|+npc, and upper bound |U|+nc) bound the true loss and are sufficiently close to guide learning (i.e., they produce useful oracle advice).
supporting_evidence: Section 5: empirical measurements of relative errors (Table 1) showing low average relative differences.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If bounds are loose in some configurations or languages (e.g., long sentences, many overlapping cycles), the oracle could provide systematically biased actions; this might lead to worse training convergence or degrade accuracy on out-of-sample data.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Sampling the first 100,000 transitions per dataset provides a representative set of configurations to estimate the tightness of the loss bounds and the behavior of the oracle.
supporting_evidence: Section 5: "we undertake the analysis of only the first 100,000 transitions on each dataset..." and Table 1 reports results over these samples.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the sampled transitions do not cover rare but important configurations (e.g., long-range non-projective interactions or late-stage cycle-prone states), the measured relative error may understate cases where bounds are poor, misleading conclusions about oracle reliability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Averaged perceptron trained with the implemented dynamic oracles is an adequate model to demonstrate the oracle's benefits; results will generalize to other scoring models (e.g., neural classifiers).
supporting_evidence: Section 6: experiments use averaged perceptron for 15 iterations and same feature templates across languages.
Conclusion: authors suggest oracle could be used with neural-network implementations.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If perceptron-specific dynamics interact with oracle approximations (e.g., sensitivity to noisy oracle labels) differently than neural models, claimed gains may not replicate under other modeling choices.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Cycle enumeration (Johnson's algorithm) to compute nc or npc is feasible enough in practice for training (for the datasets used), even though its worst-case cost depends on number of elementary cycles.
supporting_evidence: Section 4: discusses using Johnson (1975) algorithm for cycle enumeration; Section 5 applies it during bound evaluation and reports runtimes indirectly by performing the experiments.
Section 4: notes that lower-bound oracle is fastest because it avoids cycle computations.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If cycle counts explode for particular languages or sentence types, the upper-bound oracle could be prohibitively slow during training, reducing practical usefulness of the best-accuracy variant.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The deterministic cycle-breaking rule (removing the predecessor arc z→x) is the appropriate and sufficient mechanism to maintain single-head and acyclicity constraints while enabling full non-monotonic repair.
supporting_evidence: Figure 2 and textual description: transitions include subtraction of previous head arcs and of arcs that would otherwise close cycles (e.g., {k→j ∈ A | i→*k ∈ A}).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If other cycle-breaking choices (e.g., removing different arcs) would yield better reachable sets or simpler loss characterization, the chosen mechanism may limit potential repairs or introduce unnecessary complexity; correctness proofs of single-head+acyclicity preservation in all cases are not fully formalized.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Statistical significance testing over five seeds and Yeh (2000) test is adequate to assert significance of reported improvements.
supporting_evidence: Section 6: reports five experiments with different seeds and marks significance (∗ and †) using Yeh (2000).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Small number of seeds (n=5) may limit power and the validity of significance claims; differences marked as significant may be sensitive to seed selection or other experimental factors.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper builds a chain of reasoning: (1) greedy transition parsers suffer from irrecoverable past errors; (2) prior limited non-monotonic systems partially repaired errors but were restricted (projective, limited repairs); (3) Covington's non-projective parser allows revisiting words, so define full non-monotonic Left-Arc/Right-Arc that overwrite heads and deterministically break cycles by deleting a specific predecessor arc; (4) exact configuration loss for such non-monotonic system is not known to be efficiently computable, so derive a provable lower bound (|U|) and two computable upper bounds (|U|+npc and |U|+nc); (5) these bounds are empirically tight on sampled configurations (first 100k transitions per dataset), enabling an approximate dynamic oracle; (6) train perceptron models with static, monotonic-dynamic, and non-monotonic-approximate dynamic oracles and show non-monotonic variants improve average UAS/LAS on most CoNLL datasets; (7) conclude non-monotonic Covington + approximate oracle is practical and effective. I trace where the argument is well-supported (definition of transitions, loss bound inequalities, empirical tightness on sampled transitions, multi-language evaluation) and where it weakens (no formal hardness proof for exact loss, deterministic cycle-breaking rationale lacks full formal proof of correctness/uniqueness, representativeness of the 100k transition sample, runtime/practicality claims lack concrete timing profiles, unexplained Basque degradation).

Edge: motivates -> Node: Use of non-monotonicity to repair errors (Honnibal et al. 2013) but prior work limited to projective / partial repairs.
Edge: motivates -> Node: Choose Covington parser because it doesn't discard words and supports non-projectivity (Section 2).
Node: Definition — Full non-monotonic Covington transitions (Left-Arc/Right-Arc always allowed; overwrite head; deterministic cycle-break removes z→x) (Section 3, Fig.2).
Edge: requires -> Node: Need for dynamic oracle to train with error exploration (Section 4).
Node: Problem — exact loss unknown/practically infeasible for non-monotonic system (Section 4).
Edge: leads to -> Node: Derive provable lower bound |U(c,tG)| and two upper bounds |U|+npc and |U|+nc, with inequality chain |U| ≤ `(c) ≤ |U|+npc ≤ |U|+nc (Section 4).
Edge: enables -> Node: Implement approximate dynamic oracle using those bounds (Algorithm 2).
Node: Empirical bound validation — exhaustive-search comparisons on sampled transitions show low relative error (<~1% avg) for lower and closer upper bounds (Section 5, Table 1).
Edge: supports -> Node: Training experiments with perceptron across 19 languages compare static, monotonic-dynamic, and non-monotonic-approximate oracles (Section 6, Table 3).

Node: Empirical result — non-monotonic oracle (|U|+nc best) improves average UAS over monotonic on majority of languages (14/19) with some significant gains; lower bound variant is fastest in principle (Section 6).

Weak-link A: Deterministic cycle-breaking rule (remove z→x) — described but lacks formal proof that it preserves reachability properties required for correct oracle bounds (Section 3).
Weak-link B: Exact loss intractability — asserted by lack of known efficient method; no formal complexity lower bound, so claim is empirical/heuristic (Section 4).
Weak-link C: Representativeness of bound-evaluation samples — only first 100k transitions considered; generalization to all configurations or long sentences unproven (Section 5).
Weak-link D: Runtime/practicality — oracle speed claims (lower bound faster, upper slower) are logical but lack per-variant wall-clock training measurements in experiments (Section 4,6).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper defines a fully non-monotonic variant of the Covington non-projective transition system by always permitting Left-Arc/Right-Arc transitions, overwriting previous heads, and deterministically breaking cycles by deleting a specific predecessor arc. Exact configuration loss under full non-monotonicity is claimed infeasible to compute efficiently, so the authors derive a lower bound (|U|) and two upper bounds (|U|+npc and |U|+nc) on the loss, implement approximate dynamic oracles using these bounds, and empirically evaluate the tightness of the bounds and parser accuracy. Bound tightness is measured by exhaustive search on sampled transitions (first 100k) reporting relative errors typically <1%. Training experiments use averaged perceptron with standard features across 19 CoNLL languages, comparing static, monotonic-dynamic, and three non-monotonic-dynamic variants. Results: non-monotonic oracle improves average UAS over monotonic on a majority of languages (14/19) with the |U|+nc variant best on average; the |U| lower-bound oracle is claimed fastest (no cycle enumeration). Main methodological claims are plausible but depend on several key assumptions: correctness and sufficiency of the deterministic cycle-breaking rule, representativeness of the 100k-transition sampling for bound tightness, feasibility/scalability of cycle enumeration for the upper bounds, and generality of findings beyond perceptron models. Empirical evidence supports many claims but lacks wall-clock/runtime profiles, formal complexity lower bounds, proofs of correctness/uniqueness for cycle-breaking choices, deeper analysis of failure cases (e.g., Basque), and tests with different scoring architectures.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper defines a fully non-monotonic variant of the non-projective Covington transition system by (a) allowing Left-Arc/Right-Arc transitions to always create arcs, overwriting existing heads, and (b) deterministically breaking cycles by removing a specific predecessor arc when a newly-created arc would close a cycle. Because exact loss for this flexible system is not known to be efficiently computable, the authors derive a trivially-computable lower bound (|U|) and two upper bounds (|U| + npc and |U| + nc) on configuration loss, where npc counts 'problematic' cycles and nc counts all cycles in A ∪ I. These bounds form the basis of an approximate dynamic oracle. Empirically, exhaustive-search comparisons on samples (first 100k transitions per dataset) show the bounds are very tight (relative errors typically <1%), and training averaged-perceptron parsers with the non-monotonic approximate oracle improves UAS/LAS over monotonic-dynamic and static oracles on a majority of CoNLL-X/XI datasets. The lower-bound oracle is argued to be the fastest (no cycle enumeration), while the nc upper-bound variant yields the best average accuracy despite being the cruder approximation in some formal senses. Strengths include a clear algorithmic definition, practical approximate-oracle design, and multilingual empirical validation. Key caveats: (1) the deterministic cycle-breaking rule is described but not fully formalized or proven correct in all configurations (uniqueness/correctness of the removed arc is assumed), (2) no formal complexity lower bound is given for exact loss (the word 'intractable' is not proven), (3) empirical tightness and behavior are measured on the first 100k transitions only (sampling representativeness unclear), and (4) runtime/ wall-time costs per oracle variant during training are not reported, so 'practical' speed claims are qualitative. Overall, the contribution is an incremental but meaningful extension of prior non-monotonic and Covington-based work: it brings full non-monotonic repair to a non-projective parser and operationalizes approximate dynamic oracles using efficiently-computable loss bounds, but formal guarantees and broader runtime/robustness validation are still needed to reduce novelty risk.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Problem setup — greedy transition parsers suffer from irrevocable early errors; non-monotonicity can allow repair (Intro + prior work).
L2: Choose parser — non-projective Covington is suitable for full non-monotonicity because words remain accessible (Section 2/3).
L3: Define non-monotonic transitions — allow Left/Right-Arc to overwrite heads; enforce single-head by overwriting previous head (Section 3).
L4: Handle acyclicity deterministically — when new arc closes a cycle, remove predecessor z→x (Section 3, Figure 2).
L5: Loss computation problem — exact loss unknown/practically infeasible under full non-monotonicity (Section 4).
L6: Propose bounds — lower bound |U|, two upper bounds |U|+npc and |U|+nc (Section 4), with formal inequalities |U| ≤ `(c) ≤ |U|+npc ≤ |U|+nc.
L7: Practical computation — lower bound cheap; upper bounds require cycle enumeration (Johnson 1975) (Section 4).
L8: Empirical validation of bounds — exhaustive search on sampled transitions shows tightness (<1% relative error typically) (Section 5, Table 1).
L9: Build approximate dynamic oracle from bounds and train perceptron parsers (Section 4/6).

L10: Empirical parsing results — non-monotonic oracle improves accuracy over monotonic on majority of datasets; upper-bound (|U|+nc) gives best average UAS while lower bound gives fastest oracle in principle (Section 6, Table 3).
L11: Caveats and open items — Basque failure case, lack of formal proof of cycle-breaking correctness, lack of wall-time numbers, limited sample for bound evaluation (Sections 5/6/Conclusion).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper defines a fully non-monotonic variant of the non-projective Covington transition system by allowing Left-Arc and Right-Arc to always create arcs, overwriting previous heads, and resolving cycles by deterministically deleting a specific incoming arc (z→x) when a new arc x→y would create a cycle. Because exact loss for this flexible parser is not (practically) computable with known efficient methods, the authors derive a trivially-computable lower bound |U(c,tG)| (individually unreachable gold arcs under left-to-right scanning constraints) and two upper bounds: a closer upper bound that counts only 'problematic cycles' npc(A∪I) and a cruder upper bound that counts all cycles nc(A∪I). They argue |U| ≤ loss ≤ |U|+npc ≤ |U|+nc and use these bounds to build approximate dynamic oracles. Empirical evaluation (exhaustive loss computation with pruning on the first 100k transitions per dataset) shows the bounds are tight in practice (relative errors typically < 0.8%). Training averaged perceptron models using the non-monotonic approximate dynamic oracle (three variants) yields average UAS improvements over the monotonic-dynamic oracle and static baseline across CoNLL-X / X-I datasets, with the nc upper-bound variant giving the best average accuracy, and the lower-bound variant offering the fastest oracle (no cycle counting). The paper frames this as the first implementation of full non-monotonicity for a non-projective parser and the first practical approximate dynamic oracle relying on tight efficiently-computable loss approximations.
logical_argument_graph: Define full non-monotonicity for Covington: permit Left-Arc/Right-Arc always; enforce single-head by overwriting previous head; enforce acyclicity by deterministic deletion of the predecessor arc z→x when x→y would create a cycle (Section 3, Figure 2).
Note that non-monotonicity increases reachable arc sets but breaks monotonic arc-decomposability and makes exact loss hard to compute efficiently (Section 4).

Construct a lower bound |U(c,tG)| by retaining only positional reachability constraints (since single-head and cyclic restrictions can be repaired under non-monotonicity), proving it is a lower bound because these arcs are truly unreachable even with non-monotonic moves (Section 4).

Construct two upper bounds by counting cycles in A∪I(c,tG): (a) npc(A∪I) counts problematic cycles whose broken arc is a gold arc, giving a tighter upper bound; (b) nc(A∪I) counts all cycles, giving a coarser but simpler-to-evaluate bound (Section 4).

Show empirically via exhaustive-search-with-pruning on sample transitions (100k per language) that the bounds closely bracket the true loss (Table 1), making them useful to build approximate dynamic oracles (Section 5).

Train perceptron parsers with static, monotonic-dynamic, and three non-monotonic approximate dynamic oracles; report UAS/LAS across 19 datasets over 5 seeds (Table 3). Non-monotonic oracles outperform monotonic in majority of languages; nc upper-bound variant gives best average UAS; lower-bound variant is fastest in principle (Section 6).

Conclude novelty: first full non-monotonic non-projective parser and first practical approximate dynamic oracle using tight loss approximations; suggest possible transfer to neural models (Conclusion).

alternative_interpretations: The nc upper-bound variant's superior empirical accuracy may not indicate that counting all cycles is conceptually better; instead, it could reflect a regularization/inductive bias where penalizing any cycle (even harmless ones) induces behaviors that are easier for a perceptron to learn—i.e., the model benefits from a simpler surrogate objective rather than a closer loss estimate.

The tightness of bounds on sampled transitions could reflect properties of CoNLL corpora (modest sentence lengths and typical tree structures). In other corpora or constructed adversarial inputs, the bounds may be looser and oracle guidance less reliable.

The deterministic removal rule may implicitly encode a bias (favoring recent attachments) that, in some languages or annotations (e.g., free word order or many non-projective dependencies), systematically removes gold arcs more often, explaining dataset-specific drops (Basque).
transparency_notes: Experiments report averaged-per-seed UAS/LAS and statistical significance markers but do not include raw per-seed runs, standard deviations, or exact p-values—sharing per-seed results would improve reproducibility and allow meta-analysis.
No wall-clock training times, oracle call counts, or cycle-count distributions per configuration are given; adding these would substantiate practicality claims.

Implementation details (code, random seeds, software/hardware used) are not referenced in the manuscript; public code release or appendices with exact hyperparameters and timing would improve reproducibility.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Sparse precedent (prior non-monotonic work limited to projective arc-eager systems) is treated as an innovation indicator, not as evidence of correctness; novelty alone does not validate correctness—methodological soundness (proofs/diagnostics) and broader empirical validation are still required.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If deterministic cycle-breaking always removes a non-gold arc or an arc whose removal can later be repaired without blocking gold arcs, then the non-monotonic semantics and loss bounds remain valid and the approach scales.

If cycle enumeration costs remain tractable on common training corpora (cycle counts per configuration small) and lower-bound oracle accelerates training, the method will be practical for large-scale use.
If neural scoring models can learn to exploit approximate oracle labels similarly to perceptron (or better), gains will generalize beyond the experimental setup.

If Basque-like failures are due to annotation quirks or sentence-length distributions, dataset-specific preprocessing or tuned heuristics could recover gains; if due to fundamental algorithmic bias, alternative cycle-breaking strategies may be needed.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper introduces an operationally simple, fully non-monotonic semantics for a non-projective parser and couples it with an approximate-oracle design based on provable bounds—this is a new conceptual frame relative to prior restricted non-monotonic, projective work.
evidence: Introduction and Section 3: emphasis on full non-monotonicity for non-projective Covington and deterministic cycle-breaking.
Section 4: derivation of lower and two upper bounds and inequality chain used to construct approximate oracles.
uncertainty_flags: Novelty claim depends on completeness of literature search and whether unpublished/less-known prior art exists; also novelty does not imply correctness.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The algorithmic design and bounds are plausible and empirically effective on standard corpora, but key methodological gaps remain (formal correctness proofs for cycle-breaking, runtime/scale analysis, and transfer to neural models).
evidence: Table 1 and Table 3: empirical tightness and accuracy gains across many languages.
Missing: formal proof obligations and timing/scale measurements discussed in paper but not reported.
uncertainty_flags: Representative sampling and scalability beyond CoNLL tasks are untested; potential dataset-specific failure modes (Basque) need analysis.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have high confidence in empirical results reported on CoNLL datasets and in the internal logical consistency of the proposed bounds and transitions, but moderate uncertainty remains about formal correctness proofs (cycle-breaking global effects), scalability of cycle enumeration in worst-case inputs, representativeness of the sampling used for bound evaluation, and generalization to neural models. Thus a relatively high but not maximal confidence interval (0.6-0.9) reflects this balanced view.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper defines a fully non-monotonic variant of the non-projective Covington transition system by allowing Left-Arc and Right-Arc to always create arcs (overwriting previous heads) and by enforcing acyclicity via a deterministic cycle-breaking rule that removes a predecessor arc z→x when adding x→y would close a cycle. Because exact configuration loss under full non-monotonicity is not known to be efficiently computable, the authors propose a trivially-computable lower bound |U(c,tG)| and two computable upper bounds |U|+npc and |U|+nc (npc counts problematic cycles, nc counts all cycles) and implement approximate dynamic oracles using each. Empirical bound tightness (via exhaustive search with pruning) on the first 100k transitions per CoNLL dataset shows relative errors typically <1%. Training averaged-perceptron parsers with static, monotonic-dynamic, and the three non-monotonic approximate dynamic oracles across 19 languages yields that non-monotonic variants improve average UAS/LAS over monotonic on a majority of languages (14/19 for best variant), with the nc upper-bound variant giving best average accuracy and the lower bound oracle being fastest in principle (avoids cycle enumeration). Evidence in the manuscript supports most claims empirically, but several theoretical and empirical gaps remain: no formal hardness proof for exact loss, cycle-breaking uniqueness/correctness not fully formalized, representativeness of the 100k-transition sample uncertain, and runtime/practicality claims lack measured wall-clock data and scaling profiles. I flag uncertainty where the manuscript overstates implications (e.g., 'intractable' without complexity proof; 'first' without exhaustive literature cross-check).
logical_argument_graph: Greedy transition parsers suffer error propagation → dynamic oracles mitigate but are monotonic (Introduction).
Prior limited non-monotonic systems (arc-eager) had constrained repairs, mostly projective (Related work).
Covington non-projective parser revisitable structure allows defining full non-monotonic Left/Right-Arc that overwrite heads (Section 3, Fig.2).
To maintain acyclicity while permitting always-allowed arc creation, use deterministic cycle-breaking: remove predecessor z→x when x→y would form a cycle (Section 3).
Exact configuration loss unknown/practically infeasible for full non-monotonicity → derive lower bound |U| and two upper bounds |U|+npc and |U|+nc (Section 4).
Upper bounds require cycle enumeration (Johnson 1975) while lower bound is cheap (reachability checks) → tradeoff oracle cost vs accuracy (Section 4).
Empirically, bounds are tight on sampled configurations (first 100k transitions) (Section 5, Table 1).

Train perceptron with approximate dynamic oracles → non-monotonic variants give average accuracy gains over monotonic/static on many languages; best accuracy with |U|+nc, fastest training with |U| (Section 6, Table 3).

Conclude that approximate non-monotonic oracle is practical and effective; claim novelty as first full non-monotonic non-projective parser and first practical approximate dynamic oracle using close computable loss bounds (Introduction, Conclusion).

identified_claims.claim_text: A fully non-monotonic variant of the non-projective Covington transition system can be defined by allowing Left-Arc and Right-Arc transitions to always create arcs (overwriting previous heads when present) and by enforcing acyclicity deterministically by removing a specific interfering arc when a newly-created arc would form a cycle.
evidence: Section 3: textual description allowing arc creation and discarding previous attachments.
Figure 2: transition definitions include set subtraction of previous head arcs and removal of k→j such that i→*k ∈ A.
uncertainty_flags: Cycle-breaking rule is described as removing an arc z→x 'which trivially exists' but the manuscript lacks a full formal proof of uniqueness and global correctness for all configurations.
Left-to-right scanning imposes asymmetry: not all repairs (e.g., leftward repaired by rightward) are possible; limitations depend on scanning order (footnote).

identified_claims.claim_text: Exact computation of the configuration loss for the fully non-monotonic non-projective Covington parser is intractable/practically infeasible, but tight lower and upper bounds on the loss can be computed efficiently and used instead.
evidence: Section 4: authors state they "do not know of an efficient way of obtaining an exact calculation of the loss" and propose bounds |U|, |U|+npc, |U|+nc.
Section 5: empirical evaluation using exhaustive search with pruning shows bounds have low relative error on sampled configurations.
uncertainty_flags: 'Intractable' is asserted informally; no formal complexity lower bound or reduction is provided to substantiate intractability beyond practical difficulty.
Upper bounds require cycle enumeration whose worst-case cost depends on number of cycles; practical feasibility depends on typical cycle counts per dataset/sentence which are not profiled.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed lower and upper bounds are empirically very tight approximations of the true loss (relative error under ~1% on CoNLL-X / CoNLL-XI datasets when sampled over the first 100k transitions).
evidence: Table 1: reports average relative differences between bounds and exact loss, generally <0.8% for lower and 'pc upper' bounds across datasets.
Section 5: authors report 'relative errors below 0.8% in all datasets' for lower and closer upper bounds.
uncertainty_flags: Evaluation uses only first 100k transitions per dataset; representativeness of these samples for rare/adversarial configurations (long sentences, dense graphs) is uncertain.
Some datasets/languages exhibit higher error for the cruder upper bound (up to ~4% reported); language variation in tightness exists.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed approximate non-monotonic dynamic oracle (with several loss-bound variants) yields tighter reachable-arc sets than the monotonic oracle and empirically produces better parsing accuracy on a majority of CoNLL-X / CoNLL-XI datasets.
evidence: Table 3: non-monotonic variant (|U|+nc) improves UAS over monotonic on 14/19 languages; averaged UAS increases reported.
Section 6: description that non-monotonic oracles outperform monotonic on majority of datasets with several statistically significant gains.
uncertainty_flags: Statistical significance is tested over five random seeds (n=5) with Yeh (2000); small seed count may limit power/robustness of significance claims.
There is a notable negative outlier (Basque) where non-monotonic oracles perform worse; reasons not analyzed in detail, suggesting variable robustness across languages.

identified_claims.claim_label: lower bound fastest, upper bound best accuracy
identified_claims.claim_text: Using the lower-bound loss makes training faster (oracle cheaper) and still competitive, while the upper-bound variant that counts cycles gives the best average accuracy despite being a cruder approximation in some respects.
evidence: Section 4: lower bound avoids cycle enumeration, which authors state makes it the fastest option in principle.
Section 6 / Table 3: the |U|+nc variant attains the highest average UAS among compared oracles; manuscript notes lower-bound is fastest while nc upper-bound gives best average accuracy.
uncertainty_flags: No reported wall-clock training times, per-epoch oracle overheads, or cycle-enumeration runtime profiles—'faster' and 'practical' are qualitative claims unbacked by measured timings.
Scalability of Johnson's cycle enumeration on long sentences / datasets with many cycles is not empirically characterized.

identified_claims.claim_label: first full non-monotonic non-projective parser and oracle
identified_claims.claim_text: This is the first implementation of full non-monotonicity for a non-projective parsing algorithm and the first practical approximate dynamic oracle based on close, efficiently-computable loss approximations.
evidence: Introduction: authors state 'To our knowledge, the presented system is the first nonmonotonic parser that can produce non-projective dependency analyses.'
Conclusion reiterates 'To our knowledge, this is the first implementation...' and first approximate dynamic oracle using tight computable bounds.
uncertainty_flags: 'First' is an authors' claim; while plausible given cited literature (Honnibal et al. 2013; Gómez-Rodríguez & Fernández-González 2015), exhaustive cross-check beyond cited works is not provided here — risk of missing obscure prior art.
'Practical' is supported by experiments on CoNLL datasets with perceptron models but general practicality (other models, scale) remains untested.

strengths.title: Clear algorithmic definition of full non-monotonicity
strengths.description: The paper precisely specifies transition effects (head overwrite and deterministic cycle-breaking) and presents them in Figure 2, enabling reproducibility of the core algorithmic change.
evidence: Section 3: textual definition of transitions and Figure 2 showing set operations for arc removal and addition.

strengths.title: Practical approximate-oracle design grounded in bounds
strengths.description: The authors derive a simple lower bound and two upper bounds with provable inequality relations and operational algorithms that enable an approximate dynamic oracle.
evidence: Section 4: definitions of |U|, |U|+npc, |U|+nc and inequality |U| ≤ loss ≤ |U|+npc ≤ |U|+nc.
Algorithm 2: practical implementation using COUNTRELEVANTCYCLES.

strengths.title: Multilingual empirical evaluation across many datasets
strengths.description: Experiments cover 19 CoNLL datasets, comparing static, monotonic-dynamic, and three non-monotonic oracles, with averages and per-language results reported.
evidence: Section 6 and Table 3: UAS/LAS results across 19 languages with significance markers, averages, and detailed per-language numbers.

strengths.title: Empirical validation of bound tightness via exhaustive search
strengths.description: The manuscript evaluates bound quality by computing exact loss via exhaustive search with pruning on sampled transitions and reports low relative errors.
evidence: Section 5 and Table 1: results showing relative errors typically <0.8% for lower and pc upper bounds over 100k transitions per dataset.

concerns.title: Deterministic cycle-breaking correctness not fully proven
concerns.description: The paper prescribes removing a single predecessor arc z→x when adding x→y would close a cycle, but does not supply a formal proof that this deterministic choice is always unique, preserves single-head/acyclicity globally, and does not prevent building reachable gold arcs in some configurations.
evidence: Section 3: text 'we immediately remove the arc of the form z → x from A (which trivially exists, and is unique due to the single-head constraint)' but no formal theorem or proof follows.
SHARED_ANALYSIS and prior reviewers flag assumption A1/A6 concerning correctness/uniqueness.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a formal lemma and proof (or counterexample if claim fails) that removing z→x enforces acyclicity and preserves the property that any gold arc reachable under non-monotonic transitions remains reachable; alternatively, enumerate counterexamples and propose refined cycle-breaking rules or tie-breaking policies.

concerns.title: No formal complexity proof for exact loss claim
concerns.description: Authors state exact loss is 'not known to be efficiently computable' and use language suggesting intractability, but they provide no complexity-theoretic argument or reduction to justify an intractability claim.
evidence: Section 4: 'we do not know of an efficient way of obtaining an exact calculation of the loss' and repeated phrasing in Introduction/Conclusion.
SHARED_ANALYSIS flags lack of formal hardness proof.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (a) frame the statement more precisely as 'no efficient algorithm known' and avoid 'intractable', or (b) include complexity analysis or a reduction showing NP-hardness (or other lower-bound) if applicable.

concerns.title: Representativeness of 100k-transition sampling
concerns.description: Bound-tightness evaluation and exhaustive-loss experiments are limited to the first 100,000 transitions per dataset; it's unclear whether this sample covers rare but critical configurations (long sentences, dense cyclical states) that could show larger bound errors.
evidence: Section 5: explicit statement that only first 100,000 transitions analyzed; Table 1 results based on that sample.
SHARED_ANALYSIS notes sampling could underrepresent late-stage or adversarial configurations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Extend bound-tightness experiments to stratified samples: include long sentences, high-degree nodes, and randomly sampled transitions across entire training runs (not only initial 100k) and report error distributions and worst-case examples.

concerns.title: Runtime/practicality claims lack empirical timing data
concerns.description: The paper claims the lower-bound oracle makes training fastest and that upper bounds are more expensive due to cycle enumeration, but it does not provide measured wall-clock training times, per-epoch oracle overhead, or cycle-count statistics to substantiate practicality claims.
evidence: Section 4/6: qualitative statements about lower-bound being fastest and Johnson algorithm cost noted, but no timing tables or profiles.
SHARED_ANALYSIS and prior-stage reviewers recommend profiling cycle counts and training runtimes.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report wall-clock training times (total and per-epoch) for each oracle variant, average time per oracle call, distribution of cycle counts per configuration, and scalability experiments on longer sentences or larger datasets.

concerns.title: Limited analysis of failure cases and language variation
concerns.description: Basque shows an inexplicable drop in accuracy under non-monotonic oracles; the manuscript lacks analysis identifying linguistic or data-driven causes for such outliers and other variability across languages.
evidence: Section 6: 'inexplicable drop in accuracy in Basque' noted but not analyzed.
Table 3: Basque accuracy of non-monotonic variants below monotonic/static.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include targeted error analysis for Basque and other languages with divergent behavior: compare oracle decisions, cycle prevalence, sentence-length distribution, annotation idiosyncrasies, and feature interactions; report qualitative examples where non-monotonic repairs hurt accuracy.

concerns.title: 'First' novelty claims need cautious phrasing and literature check
concerns.description: Authors claim this is the first non-monotonic non-projective parser and first practical approximate dynamic oracle with tight computable bounds; while plausible, the assertion rests on 'to our knowledge' and should be hedged unless exhaustive prior-art search is demonstrated.
evidence: Introduction/Conclusion: 'To our knowledge, this is the first...'
Prior-stage reviewers note possibility of missing obscure prior works.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Soften 'first' claims (e.g., 'to our knowledge, no prior work has implemented full non-monotonicity for a non-projective parser') or add a brief literature survey explicitly stating search scope and why earlier related works differ.

concerns.title: Generality to other scoring models untested
concerns.description: All experiments use averaged perceptron; the paper conjectures applicability to neural models but provides no empirical evidence that oracle approximations behave similarly under different scoring architectures.
evidence: Section 6 / Conclusion: experiments use perceptron; suggestion that oracle could be used with neural models is left as future work.
ASSUMPTION A4 in shared analysis flags this.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either add preliminary experiments with a simple neural classifier (e.g., feedforward or stack-LSTM) on a subset of languages or clarify limitations and scope of conclusions to perceptron-based training.

concerns.title: Statistical testing over limited seeds
concerns.description: Significance is reported using five random seeds; small sample size reduces statistical power and may make significance markers sensitive to outliers.
evidence: Section 6: 'we run five experiments with different seeds' and use Yeh (2000) to mark significance.
SHARED_ANALYSIS notes n=5 may limit power.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either increase number of random seeds (e.g., 10+) or report confidence intervals and effect sizes per language to complement p-value style markers.

uncertainty_flags: No formal complexity-theoretic proof that exact loss is intractable; phrasing should avoid implying formal intractability without proof.
Cycle-breaking rule uniqueness and preservation of reachability assumptions are not proven formally (A1/A6 unresolved).
Bound tightness evaluated on first 100k transitions; representativeness for whole state space unconfirmed (A3).
No measured wall-clock training times or per-oracle-call cost reported—runtime/practicality claims are qualitative.
Generality to neural or other scoring models is conjectural and untested (A4).
Statistical significance over five seeds is limited in power; effect sizes and confidence intervals not reported (A7).
alternative_interpretations: The deterministic cycle-breaking rule may be a pragmatic heuristic that works well empirically on CoNLL datasets but could fail on constructed adversarial inputs; the empirical tightness of bounds may stem from data-specific low cycle densities rather than fundamental property of non-monotonic Covington.

The observed accuracy gains may be partially attributable to increased expressivity/noise in oracle labels that better match perceptron training dynamics; gains could shrink or change direction under different learners (e.g., neural models) or hyperparameter regimes.

The nc upper-bound giving best accuracy despite being cruder could indicate that penalizing all cycles acts as a useful regularizer for the learned model (simpler objective easier to approximate), rather than that nc better approximates the true loss.

However, concrete runtime measurements (wall-clock) and per-configuration cycle-count distributions are missing; adding those would substantially increase transparency about practicality claims.
The 'first' novelty assertions depend on literature coverage; authors should explicitly document search scope to increase transparency.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Sparse precedent for full non-monotonic non-projective parsing in the retrieved corpus suggests novelty, but novelty alone does not guarantee theoretical correctness or practical robustness—both must be independently validated.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If deterministic cycle-breaking is provably correct (or at least correct in all practical configurations encountered in real data), then bounds and oracle will be sound and the method can scale.

If cycle counts per configuration remain low in practice across languages and sentence lengths, Johnson-based cycle enumeration will be tractable and the nc variant's runtime overhead will be acceptable.

If the perceptron learning dynamics that benefit from approximate oracle guidance transfer to modern neural models (or if similar approximations are used as training losses), the approach could yield gains in stronger architectures.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Builds directly on prior non-monotonic (arc-eager) and non-projective dynamic oracle work (Gómez-Rodríguez & Fernández-González 2015) by combining full non-monotonic repairs with non-projective Covington and operational approximate oracles—an extension that is technically non-trivial and useful.
evidence: Paper compares to monotonic dynamic oracle for Covington and cites prior limited non-monotonic arc-eager systems.
uncertainty_flags: Depends on confirming deterministic cycle-breaking correctness and representativeness of empirical results across other modeling choices.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Potentially disruptive but requires further validation
novelty_lenses.rationale: If the non-monotonic design and efficient approximate oracle generalize to modern neural parsers and large-scale corpora, the approach could change how greedy non-projective parsers are trained by enabling systematic repair; currently, evidence is promising but limited to perceptron experiments and CoNLL datasets.
evidence: Empirical improvements across many languages and tightness of bounds on sampled configurations suggest practical viability.
uncertainty_flags: No experiments with neural models, no runtime scaling data, and unproven theoretical properties limit immediate disruptive impact.

confidence_interval.rationale: High confidence in reported empirical results on CoNLL datasets for perceptron training (tables and exhaustive-sampling methods provided), medium confidence in claims about general practicality, theoretical intractability, and universal correctness of cycle-breaking due to missing formal proofs and runtime/representativeness data.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a clear, implementable definition of a fully non-monotonic variant of the Covington non-projective transition system (Left-Arc/Right-Arc always allowed, head-overwrite semantics, deterministic cycle-breaking via predecessor-arc removal).

Exact configuration loss under full non-monotonicity is not known to admit a known efficient exact algorithm; the authors propose a provable lower bound (|U|) and two computable upper bounds (|U|+npc and |U|+nc) with the inequality chain |U| ≤ loss ≤ |U|+npc ≤ |U|+nc.

Empirical experiments (exhaustive-search-with-pruning on sampled transitions and perceptron training on CoNLL-X/XI) show that the proposed bounds are empirically tight on the sampled configurations and that non-monotonic approximate dynamic oracles typically improve parsing accuracy over the monotonic oracle on a majority of tested languages.

There is a practical trade-off: the lower-bound oracle avoids cycle enumeration and is argued to be faster in principle; the nc upper-bound (counting all cycles) gives the best average accuracy in the reported perceptron experiments.

The work appears to be a meaningful incremental contribution combining full non-monotonic repair with non-projective Covington and practical approximate oracles, and includes multilingual empirical evaluation and algorithmic pseudocode that aid reproducibility.
disagreements: Whether the deterministic cycle-breaking rule (remove the predecessor arc z→x when adding x→y would create a cycle) is formally correct and sufficient: multiple reviewers flag the absence of a formal proof that this choice preserves reachability of gold arcs in all configurations; some treat it as a plausible operational rule that works empirically, others consider the lack of formal invariants a major methodological gap.

The characterization of exact loss as 'intractable': reviewers agree no efficient exact method is demonstrated, but disagree about the strength of the authors' wording—several reviewers request a formal complexity argument or softer phrasing, while others accept the empirical infeasibility observed in practice.

Practicality/runtime claims: reviewers concur conceptually that the lower-bound oracle is cheaper and upper bounds costlier (due to cycle enumeration), but disagree about whether the paper substantiates 'faster' and 'practical' with sufficient empirical runtime measurements—most request wall-clock/profiling evidence; none treat the qualitative statements as fully proven.

Generality of empirical gains to other scoring models: reviewers diverge on importance—some see perceptron-based gains as adequate proof-of-concept (incremental novelty), while others insist that testing with at least one neural scoring model is necessary to claim broader practical impact.
uncertainty_hotspots: Formal correctness and uniqueness of the deterministic cycle-breaking removal (assumptions A1/A6): lacking a formal lemma/proof; potential edge cases where the removed arc might be needed later could invalidate reachability-based bounds.

Representativeness of the sampled configurations used to evaluate bound tightness (first 100k transitions per dataset): sampling may underrepresent late-stage, long-sentence, or high-cycle-density states where bounds could be substantially looser.

Scalability and runtime behavior of cycle enumeration (Johnson's algorithm) for the upper-bound oracles in worst-case or atypical corpora: the paper lacks measured wall-clock training times, per-oracle overhead, and cycle-count distributions.
Statistical robustness of reported significance: experiments use five random seeds (n=5), which limits power and sensitivity to seed choice for per-language significance claims.
Generality of results across model families: only averaged perceptron experiments are reported; behavior under neural scoring architectures (modern parsers) is uncertain.
model_diversity_effects: Architecture interaction: reviewers note that perceptron learning dynamics may interact with approximate oracle labels differently than neural optimizers; the observed gains might partly derive from perceptron-specific behavior (e.g., tolerance to certain label noise or benefit from richer exploration), so replication with neural models could change effect sizes or directions.

Oracle signal bias: the three loss-bound variants impose different inductive biases—lower bound is permissive, nc upper-bound is conservative (penalizes all cycles). These biases may favor different learners: simpler, conservative signals (nc) may act as regularizers that neural models handle differently than perceptron.

Role-specific effects: as a training-time component, the oracle's approximation error interacts with the scorer's capacity. High-capacity models may amplify small systematic biases in the oracle (either positive or negative), while low-capacity models may benefit more from stronger, simpler surrogate signals (explaining why cruder nc gave best average accuracy with perceptron).

Language/genre sensitivity: model-oracle interactions may be more sensitive on languages with abundant non-projectivity or annotation peculiarities (e.g., Basque), leading to dataset-specific divergences that depend on both oracle behavior and model inductive biases.
meta_review.editor_guidance: When assessing the manuscript's contribution and revision needs, prioritize verification of algorithmic invariants and empirical robustness rather than reweighing reviewers into a single accept/reject metric. Core technical issues to request from authors before a final decision: (1) a formal statement (lemma/theorem) and proof or exhaustive characterization concerning the deterministic cycle-breaking rule—specifically uniqueness of the predecessor arc to be removed and preservation (or precise limitation) of reachable gold arcs; (2) empirical wall-clock/runtime measurements for oracle variants (per-oracle-call cost, per-epoch training time, and total training time) and profiling of cycle counts (average, median, and tails) across datasets and sentence lengths; (3) expanded bound-tightness experiments using stratified sampling including long sentences, high-cycle-density trees, and late-stage configurations, with distributions of relative error, not only averages; (4) at least a small-scale replication with a neural scoring model (1–3 diverse languages) or, if impractical, a careful argumentation about why perceptron results should generalize and what failure modes to expect; (5) a focused error analysis for notable outliers (e.g., Basque) identifying why non-monotonic variants underperformed and whether mitigations exist. Keep the novelty claim phrased cautiously (e.g., 'to our knowledge') and request an expanded related-work check. These items will materially reduce epistemic uncertainty and help the editor judge practical significance and correctness.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewers' substantive concerns, please provide the following updates: (1) Formalize the cycle-breaking mechanism: add a clear lemma stating the invariant(s) maintained when removing the predecessor arc (existence/uniqueness of z, effect on reachability), and include either a proof or empirical/constructive counterexamples plus mitigations. If full proof is elusive, characterize exact conditions where it holds and discuss implications. (2) Clarify the wording around exact loss 'intractability': either provide a complexity-theoretic argument or soften language to 'no known efficient method; expensive in practice' and add stress tests illustrating practical blow-up. (3) Empirically substantiate practicality: report wall-clock times (per-epoch and total) for each oracle variant, average time per oracle call, and cycle-enumeration runtime and counts (mean, median, 90/99 percentiles) across datasets and sentence-length bins. (4) Expand bound-tightness validation: evaluate bounds on stratified and randomized samples beyond the first 100k transitions (include long sentences and high-cycle cases) and report error distributions and worst-case examples. (5) Provide a focused investigation of failure cases (Basque): include diagnostics (cycle prevalence, sentence lengths, annotation patterns, examples of harmful cycle-breaking) and, if applicable, proposed fixes or caveats. (6) Demonstrate generality: add at least one small experiment pairing the non-monotonic oracle with a neural greedy scorer on a subset of languages, or clearly argue why perceptron results should generalize and which limitations remain. Finally, release code and scripts or add an appendix with implementation details, seeds used, and environment/timing measurement methodology to maximize reproducibility.

strengths: Concrete, implementable definition of full non-monotonic Covington transitions with explicit set-operator semantics (Figure 2) and pseudocode (Algorithms 1–2).

Claim that exact loss computation is 'intractable/practically infeasible' is not supported by a formal complexity-theoretic hardness proof or reduction; the argument rests on lack of known efficient algorithms and empirical difficulty rather than a proven lower bound.

Bound-tightness experiments use only the first 100,000 transitions per dataset; representativeness for late-stage, long-sentence, or high-cycle-density configurations is uncertain and could hide cases where bounds are looser.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Traditionally, the negation word is determined from a small hand- 727 Kiritchenko, Zhu, & Mohammad crafted list (Taboada et al., 2011). The scope of negation is often assumed to begin from the word following the negation word until the next punctuation mark or the end of the sentence (Polanyi & Zaenen, 2004; Kennedy & Inkpen, 2005). More sophisticated methods to detect the scope of negation through semantic parsing have also been proposed (Li, Zhou, Wang, & Zhu, 2010). A common way to capture the impact of negation is to reverse the polarities of the sentiment words in the scope of negation. Taboada et al.
